articles.title: 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team
articles.content: Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting. Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague. “Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains . “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.” As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool. Real teenage engineering Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools. “I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.” He developed Autark - or, more accurately, prompted AI coding tools to do it for him - to come up with a tool that could fulfill that want. You know what that means: It’s capable, but that capability also makes it dangerous. Autark’s page on access and data makes clear what’s at risk if you give it unfettered access to a PC, and why you don’t want to let the thing run roughshod over a system. “It can do everything,” the page explains , because “Autark does not put walls around its agents.” There’s no sandboxing in Autark, no approval prompts, and no permission gates. It doesn’t stop agents from spending all the money they can get their hands on, deleting files, or sending unsolicited emails, either. Agents run with the privileges of the machine's user, with approval checks and permission restrictions disabled or bypassed. Even the safety limit parley that users have with Autark establishes guidelines, not rules. “The first thing the AI asks is how far it may go,” the access page points out. “That is a question, not a technical barrier.” That means agents given a task that conflicts with their stated limits may still attempt to carry it out. As we’ve seen in recent months , some AI agents have found ways around restrictions, instructions be damned. “In our own live test runs, agents given a vague request reached real repositories, backups, SSH keys and .env files within minutes, and one changed the permissions of a file it had found,” the access page notes. In other words, it’s probably best to stick Autark on a machine that doesn’t contain anything you’d want to avoid losing - even Hees admits as much. “I would not claim that … the app is suitable for unattended access to sensitive systems,” the teen dev told us. That’s not to say Autark lacks protections for secrets, though. Autark’s site explains that stored passwords and keys are encrypted and referred to using IDs that keep their values out of prompts. It also says its servers don't store user data, with a meeting server used to relay encrypted traffic between devices. If you're willing to try Autark to see whether it can improve your workflows, you don't need to rely on its servers. While prepackaged apps are available from Autark’s website, it’s also fully open source and available on GitHub . Everything, even the meeting server code, is available for self-hosting and modification under an Apache open source license. The…

articles.title: Fintech giant Plaid opening Seattle engineering office, with plans to double local headcount
articles.content: A South Lake Union view from Plaid’s Seattle office at 1000 Dexter Ave. N. (Plaid Photo) Plaid is opening an engineering office in Seattle’s Westlake neighborhood in January and plans to double its local workforce to about 80 people by next summer. The San Francisco-based fintech company says the new 11,466-square-foot space at 1000 Dexter Ave. N. will serve as a hub for its technical teams, with most open Seattle roles focused on machine learning, data science and engineering. Plaid said in a blog post that it chose Seattle because much of the cloud and AI technology behind modern financial infrastructure was built in the region. The company is developing AI models trained on its network to understand patterns in how money moves. Plaid already has about 40 employees in the Seattle area, who currently work remotely, The Seattle Times reported. “There’s just great talent in Seattle, so it’s a little bit of a no-brainer for us,” Meghan Welch, Plaid’s chief people officer, told the Times. Zachary Perret, co-founder and CEO of fintech company Plaid. (LinkedIn Photo) Plaid’s careers page lists more than 50 open roles that include Seattle as a possible location, though most are also open in San Francisco, New York or other cities. About half are in data, engineering or security, with the rest spread across sales, legal, finance and other teams. Founded in 2013, Plaid was valued at $8 billion in an employee share sale earlier this year, down from a 2021 peak of $13.4 billion. The company says more than 150 million people have used its technology to connect their financial accounts. Plaid is led by co-founder and CEO Zachary Perret . The new office will have views of Lake Union, an outdoor deck and event space, along with three catered meals a day, according to the company.

articles.title: Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in
articles.content: A Sabey Data Center facility in Quincy, Wash. (GeekWire Photo / Lisa Stiffler) Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become. Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press . The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities. So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest. “We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers , in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.” Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate. Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks. A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon. Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio , D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed. Doglio has been meeting with stakeholders, including tech companies and data center developers, and will try again in the coming legislative session under noticeably different conditions. Fellow lawmakers, she said, will take on AI’s intersection with privacy, education, labor and other issues. “It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said. Inside a Microsoft data center. (Microsoft Photo) More outreach, bigger obstacles Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears. In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative , which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs. Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program , pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs. Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience. “It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030. But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new…

articles.title: I tested the Google Pixel Tag and it’s the most findable tracker for Android phones — plus it does something Apple AirTag can't
articles.content: Over the past few years, I’ve tested my fair share of Bluetooth trackers — ranging from wallet-thin cards like the Statik SmartCard Incognito to the Pebblebee Halo , which can potentially help elderly individuals in emergency situations. Google has expanded its Find Hub network, finally giving Android users plenty of options, but many of these trackers share one glaring limitation: pinpoint proximity tracking. While iPhone users have long enjoyed the superb performance of Precision Finding — leaning on Ultra Wideband (UWB) for pinpoint accuracy — most Android trackers don’t have that luxury. Instead, they rely on basic Bluetooth proximity that only shows broad geographic circles on a map. Google’s Pixel Tag is one of the few Android trackers that packages Ultra Wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth Channel Sounding directly into Google’s native ecosystem. As a result, the Pixel Tag delivers true visual Precision Finding to Android devices. After putting it to the test, I found it holds one distinct advantage over the AirTag and one of the best Bluetooth trackers you can get. Google Pixel Tag review: Cheat Sheet What is it? The Pixel Tag is Google’s first Bluetooth tracker, combining Ultra Wideband (UWB) precision finding with the global Find Hub network to help track it down. Who is it for? For Android users who want seamless, AirTag-like pinpoint tracking to locate their keys, bags, wallets, and other gear. What does it cost? A single Pixel Tag fetches for $29, or $99 for a four-pack. What do we like? We love its class-leading Precision Finding range, slim 5.4mm wallet-friendly profile, persistent low-battery alerts, and the ability to reverse-ring a misplaced phone. What don't we like? It lacks a native keyring hole and the very limited selection of accessories at launch. Google Pixel Tag review : Specifications Google Pixel Tag Price $29 (1-pack) / $99 (4-pack) Dimensions 28 x 46.1 x 5.4 mm Weight 0.4 ounces (11.8 grams) Materials Stainless steel & polycarbonate Water/Dust Resistance IP67 Reverse Phone Finding Yes (Built-in button) Location Tech Ultra-Wideband (UWB) + Bluetooth Channel Sounding Battery Type User-replaceable CR2032 coin cell Battery Life Up to 1 year Tracking Network Google Find Hub Item Sharing Up to 10 users Google Pixel Tag review: The ups Outstanding Precision Finding range John Velasco / Tom's Guide John Velasco / Tom's Guide John Velasco / Tom's Guide Easily the best feature of the Pixel Tag is its ability to lock down an exact position with outstanding Precision Finding range, which actually managed to outperform even Apple's AirTag 2 in my testing. Using the Find My Device app on an Android phone, you get intuitive on-screen visual guidance, complete with compass-like directional arrows and real-time distance readouts that point you right where you need to go. While the AirTag 2 tapped out around 74 feet in my testing before dropping its Ultra Wideband connection, the Pixel Tag held on slightly farther, reaching roughly 82 feet. That extra reach eliminates the guesswork of tracking down misplaced gear, like my keys when I've completely forgotten where I left them. Plus, you can still trigger a loud audio chime if the tag slips deep between couch cushions and you can't spot it right away. Thinner design than the AirTag (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) The AirTag has an unmistakable look, but Google has delivered an equally compelling design — especially when it comes to size. At just 5.4mm thick, the Pixel Tag is significantly sleeker than the AirTag, making it far less conspicuous when slipped into a standard wallet. With its minimalist, matte-finished polycarbonate body, I really dig the pebble-like aesthetic, which does a far better job of masking smudges and fingerprints than the AirTag's scratch-prone stainless steel back. articles.title: Autonomous treasury agents: How Trovata built an AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore
articles.content: Corporate treasury teams face a persistent challenge: fragmented banking data scattered across dozens of bank portals, manual reporting trapped in spreadsheets, and legacy Treasury Management Systems (TMS) that can’t scale for modern enterprise needs. For treasury teams these manual processes create delays, errors, and an inability to make real-time cash decisions when they matter most. Trovata is an AI-native cash and liquidity management platform with direct connections to over 10,000 banks, serving enterprises globally from a single cloud-based platform. In 2023, Trovata launched the first generative AI built specifically for treasury. Now, with Trovata’s latest AI-native updates, they’ve evolved from delivering insights to deploying autonomous agents that act on behalf of treasury teams. Trovata’s customers have seen measurable results: $1M+ in annualized cost savings, over 5 hours per day saved per accounting team, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS costs, and treasury reporting reduced from hours or days to under a minute. In this post, we explore how Trovata built autonomous treasury agents on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the architecture secured with role-based access control (RBAC) that supports bank-branded AI deployment, and how agentic workflows are transforming corporate treasury from manual operations to real-time decision-making at enterprise scale. Solution overview Trovata operates as an AI-native treasury operating system, providing direct connections to over 10,000 banks through a single system for cash reporting, forecasting, analysis, and money movement. Treasury teams today face a three-pressure problem: Fragmented banking data across multiple portals, requiring manual aggregation and reconciliation. Manual reporting and reconciliation consuming hours or even days of skilled team members’ time. Legacy TMS applications that lack cloud-native architecture and AI capabilities needed for modern operations. Trovata’s evolution from its first generative AI for treasury in 2023 to its AI-native capabilities with autonomous agents represents a fundamental shift. The solution moves from static insights to persistent agentic workflows that operate continuously on behalf of treasury teams. Critically, Trovata AI is built directly into the treasury operating system. It’s not a generic chatbot layered on top, but embedded intelligence tied to real treasury objects with a governed path to automation through agents. Trovata chose AWS for this transformation for three reasons. Its serverless, cloud-native infrastructure supports real-time execution, Amazon Bedrock provides large language model (LLM) inference for natural language queries and AI features, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore handles agent orchestration with RBAC security, rapid deployment, and global scale. The core AWS services powering Trovata’s AI-native solution include: Amazon Bedrock – LLM inference for natural language understanding and generation. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Agent orchestration, agentic workflows, and RBAC security. Serverless AWS infrastructure – Real-time execution at enterprise scale. Architecture diagram The Trovata AI architecture centers on autonomous treasury agents operating within a bank-branded, RBAC-secured framework. The solution comprises several key components working together: Trovata AI Chat – Natural language querying of multi-bank treasury data, so users can ask questions like “What was our net cash position across all accounts yesterday?” and receive instant, accurate responses. AI Insights – Automated anomaly detection, variance explanation, and trend analysis that surfaces critical information proactively. AI Agents – Persistent workflows running on schedules, triggers, or rules to monitor activity, explain variance, detect anomalies, and deliver updates automatically, without human intervention. articles.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
articles.content: Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without s everywhere, ` ` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0]) Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent +JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge. 200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1] I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU. We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.) People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided. Try it out: DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler! articles.title: Eight Sleep Pod 6 vs Orion vs Bear Elite Hybrid: Which cooling mattress is really worth your money this Black Friday? We've lab tested them all and here's our recommendation for every type of sleeper
articles.content: Eight Sleep Pod 6 Type: Smart mattress cover Sizes: 6 (twin–Cal king) Sleep trial: 30 nights Warranty: 2 years Subscription: Yes (from $17/month) Price (on sale): From $1,899 at Eight Sleep Orion Sleep System Type: Smart mattress cover Sizes: 3 (queen–Cal king) Sleep trial: 30 nights Warranty: 2 years Subscription: Optional ($250/year) Price (on sale): From $1,795 at Orion Bear Elite Hybrid Mattress Type: Hybrid mattress Sizes: 7 (twin–Split king) Sleep trial: 365 nights Warranty: Limited lifetime Subscription: No Price (on sale): From $1,298 at Bear Just yesterday I was sweating through a scorching summer night and now when I climb into bed, it’s like stepping into an igloo. Either way is bad news for my sleep and can result in 3 a.m. wake-ups. No wonder all the best mattresses we’ve tried have passed rigorous temperature regulation tests. The best cooling mattresses use heat dissipating materials to kick out night sweats and counteract heatwaves so you’re able to snooze soundly. And when it comes to cooling beds, the Bear Elite Hybrid is the best we’ve ever tested. But recently I’ve been hands-on with the Eight Sleep Pod 6 and Orion Sleep System, two of the best smart mattresses that use active cooling to create even temperatures. These high-tech systems deliver impressive hands-on cooling but at a high price. So in the Black Friday mattress and sleep sales , which should you buy? I'm here to advise you based on our extensive testing and my own experience with all three cooling beds. Eight Sleep vs Orion vs Bear Elite: Price & deals The Eight Sleep and Orion are premium smart mattress covers The Bear Elite Hybrid is an upper mid-range hybrid mattress Eight Sleep requires a subscription, Orion and Bear don't The Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the most expensive of the three, with a queen coming in at $2,899 MSRP. The Orion is cheaper with an MSRP of $2,395. The Bear Elite Hybrid has an MSRP of $2,284 for a queen, but regular Bear mattress sales can knock it as low as $1,370.40. Keep in mind, both the Eight Sleep Pod 6 and the Orion are covers only. The Elite Hybrid is the only option that's actually a mattress. As well as being the priciest upfront, the Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the only one with a mandatory subscription. Starting at $17/month, it includes sleep tracking and is essential for operating the Pod. Orion also has a sleep tracking subscription but it's optional (although more expensive at $250/year). Bear, of course, is subscription-free. Bear blows both smart covers out of the water when it comes to benefits, offering a 365-night sleep trial and a limited lifetime warranty. Orion and Eight Sleep both offer just a 30-night trial and 2-year warranty. Pod 6 (queen): was $2899 now $2699 With the launch of the Pod 6, Eight Sleep expanded into twin sizes, offering more options for solo sleepers. A twin is now only $1,899 (was $1,999) while there's $200 off larger sizes. Eight Sleep sales are never blockbusters so this is a noteworthy price drop, although we're hopeful more discounts will appear before Black Friday. View Deal Sleep System (queen): was $2395 now $1795 A queen-size smart mattress cover for under $2,000 is a rare bargain and in the Orion Black Friday sale there's up to $600 off this climate control system. Sizes are limited (just queen, king, and Cal king as of writing) but the price is fantastic. A bigger discount is unlikely, so now's the time to shop. View Deal Elite Hybrid (queen): was $2284 now $1370.40 The Bear Elite Hybrid sells at a competitive price for a cooling hybrid mattress, particularly one with a luxury pillow-top. There's usually 30% off at Bear but keep an eye out for the 35% off deal that reliably appears over the holidays. Right now, though, you can get 40% off plus free accessories when you use our TOMS40 code at the checkout, bringing the price of a queen down to $1,370.40. articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.content: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally. A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory. Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array. This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected. The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied. Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git. Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute. The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges. The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git…

articles.title: Blender 5.3 Released With Nvidia DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction, Vulkan Default
articles.content: Blender 5.3 has been released with support for 3D Gaussian Splats, Nvidia DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction and Vulkan as the default graphics backend on Linux. Phoronix reports: Blender now allows importing Gaussian Splats from PLY, SPZ, and glTF files. Also new to Blender 5.3 is NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support as a new denoiser. Blender 5.3 also brings support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices. For the Cycles code in Blender 5.3 the Principled BSDF for shader nodes now supports dispersion. Another notable change with Blender 5.3 is the Vulkan back-end now being the default on Windows (except for Windows on ARM) and Linux systems. Vulkan 1.1 or newer is required and should deliver better performance than OpenGL. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Microsoft lobbies against potential ban on Chinese optical networking gear for AI data centers as FCC mulls restricting imports
articles.content: Microsoft, the tech giant that is building 35 data centers around the U.S. and has plans for 134 more, has reportedly met with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the National Security Council as the FCC is considering an import ban on Chinese optical transceivers . According to Reuters , the company, alongside the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), is lobbying against the move. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible “It really threatens to arguably grind (the data center rollout) to a halt,” ITI Executive Vice President of Policy and General Counsel John Miller said. He also added, “Those chips, without optical transceivers, literally could just sit there waiting around unutilized until you actually have the transceivers to essentially connect them together,” referring to the AI chips that data centers use. Optical transceivers are tiny modules plugged into hardware that convert their electrical signals into light signals, allowing data to be transmitted as light pulses across fiber optics. Data centers increasingly use optical transceivers and fiber optics to transmit data between AI GPUs and server racks, as they’re faster, offer lower latency, require less power, and generate less heat compared to traditional copper connections. However, Chinese companies currently supply 66% of the global market, meaning banning them from supplying data centers in the U.S. would more than halve the available supply, thereby exacerbating the various shortages that have been pummeling the industry . However, there are concerns that some of these transceivers could be compromised by Beijing and be used to steal data, install malware, or remotely disrupt American data centers, which is why the FCC is considering the restriction, just like how it banned Huawei from the U.S. telecommunications network. But unlike Huawei, which had many established competitors in the telecommunications hardware industry, only two U.S.-based companies produce optical transceivers that data centers need — Coherent and Lumentum. While these firms could produce optical transceivers to compete with Chinese offerings, they simply do not have the scale to make up for the shortfall if the FCC bans Chinese imports today. One compromise floated by the Trump administration is that it would only ban Chinese optical transceivers capable of hitting 3.2 terabits per second. While this technology already exists, its production isn’t expected to expand until 2028, with installation not beginning until 2029. This should give American producers time to ramp up their own output, although the suggestion is still under consideration.

articles.title: Three China-Nexus Espionage Campaigns Linked Through Sparrow Malware Ecosystem

articles.title: AMD VP and chief Zen architect rebuke claims that Nvidia and Arm made CPUs for agentic AI — ‘We didn’t magically know four years ago that agentic was going to be a thing’
articles.content: Two prominent voices within AMD agree that the company didn’t design its new Zen 6 family, codenamed Venice, explicitly for agentic AI in a clear shot at Nvidia and Arm, who’ve both described their latest data center CPUs as “agentic” in nature. In separate talks, AMD’s chief Zen architect Mike Clark and corporate VP Madhu Rangarajan said that the company didn’t predict the agentic wave when Zen 6 development started. Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms CPU scaling with DLSS Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent We just wrapped up testing AMD's Venice CPUs, which you can read more about in our Zen 6 benchmarking article . CPU development cycles are measured in years, and given that the agentic frenzy around CPUs hit around March of this year, it’s unreasonable to expect that anyone has developed silicon specifically for agentic AI, much less a general-purpose data center CPU. And still, Nvidia claims its Vera CPU was “purpose-built” for agentic AI, while Arm says its AGI CPU was “designed for the demands of agentic AI.” “We think that the EPYC 9006 CPU is the best CPU for the agentic era, and spoiler alert, we didn’t magically know four years ago that agentic was going to be a thing and purpose-built something for agentic,” said Rangarajan in a session with media. “The reality is an agentic workflow is a diverse set of tasks… and in order to execute those tasks well, you need compute that is able to handle a diverse set of workloads with a full portfolio.” Introducing the Zen 6 microarchitecture, Mike Clark agreed with the sentiment: “I’m not going to mislead and act like I knew agentic computing was coming, or we knew it, but we did strongly believe that the CPU would always have a place in the software ecosystem of AI… And as agentic [has] blown up, we [are] able to now deploy that for agentic compute workloads.” As AMD rolls out its next-generation microarchitecture with Venice CPUs, it’s targeting the messaging from Arm and Nvidia, which have posed the most direct threat to AMD’s continued rise in the data center on the back of agentic workloads. And indeed, there are performance vectors where Nvidia’s Vera looks strong for agentic workloads, as you can see in our Nvidia Vera testing . AMD’s argument, however, is that agentic AI calls for a broad range of CPUs just as general-purpose workloads do, pushing back on the single-SKU approach of Nvidia and Arm. Our testing of two AMD Venice chips supports that argument, as well, with the dense EPYC 9996 with its 256 cores and 512 threads offering peak throughput performance, while the frequency-optimized EPYC 9686F goes toe-to-toe with Vera in the role of an AI host node. AMD is launching two additional ranges next year, with Venice-X targeting HPC with its 3D-stack cache, and Verano going directly after Vera as an AI host node with an LPDDR5X memory system. Although the workload characteristics of agentic AI are still in the process of being defined, we have a better understanding of how those loops work now than we did at the beginning of the year. And like all complex topics, the answer to what is important in a CPU for agentic AI is the always-disappointing “it depends.” As we break down in our early testing procedure for agentic AI , the workload characteristics and demand on the CPU/memory are defined by what the agent is doing, and in the data center, what several agents are doing at high concurrency when sandboxed. A coding agent will generally call more tools that are taxing on the CPU than a web browsing agent, for example, while an agent that queries a database may call for strong memory performance. articles.title: AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ deep dive and benchmarking
articles.content: AMD’s EPYC ‘Venice’ CPUs are the first to debut the new Zen 6 architecture, and we’ve been testing two chips from the range over the past several weeks to see how they compare to Nvidia’s Vera, and more broadly, how the Zen 6 architecture departs from Zen 5 ahead of the expected consumer-focused Olympic Ridge launch next year. Zen 5 was a ground-up redesign of AMD’s storied Zen core, and Zen 6 takes that foundation and expands it in just about every regard. Zen 6 uses TSMC’s N2P node, but it also comes with significant architectural changes under the hood. Within the core, a redesigned vector engine pushes AMD’s SIMD performance even higher, and it now natively supports half-precision FP16 instructions alongside full, 32-bit precision. It also splits integer schedulers within the execution engine, allowing for more instructions in flight through the core. Across the die, AMD made other significant changes. The single IOD of previous generations is now split across two IODs, giving the SP7 platform access to 16 memory channels (though at the cost of PCIe 6.0 lanes compared to the previous generation and SP8 platform). The CCDs have been upgraded, too, for the first time since Zen 3. A standard Zen 6 CCD can now scale up to 12 cores, while a Zen 6c packs 32 cores. With Zen 5 and 5c, CCDs topped out at eight cores and 16 cores, respectively. For the Zen 6c CCD, AMD also doubled the amount of shared L3 per core, which effectively quadruples the L3 compared to Zen 5c, since the CCD packs twice the number of cores. Interestingly, Zen 6 is neither a marginal optimization to Zen 5, nor a complete architecture redesign. Stepping back, it looks like AMD pushes as many dials as it has access to to their highest level, and that holds up looking at performance. The 256-core EPYC 9996 delivers 1,024 threads in a 2P configuration, which came out 93% ahead of the 768-thread 2P EPYC 9965 server we tested in SPEC CPU 2026’s intrate throughput test. The frequency-optimized EPYC 9686F excels elsewhere, notably in scientific computing and HPC workloads, and it serves as AMD’s competitor to Vera, at least before the LPDDR-based Verano platform arrives from AMD next year. AMD says it believes Venice is fundamentally a generation ahead of the competition, which would be a worthless line if it wasn’t backed up by data. Intel’s Granite Rapids-AP is rarely in the conversation, and although Vera maintains some competitive positions , Venice is often ahead — sometimes orders of magnitude ahead. Intel’s Diamond Rapids is set to launch next year, which should help balance the scales. But AMD has set an incredibly high bar with Venice, one that it will likely extend even higher for some workloads with the arrival of Venice-X and Verano next year . There’s a lot to get to here. We have a full deep dive into the Zen 6 microarchitecture, a broader look at the chip itself, the platform(s) AMD is pushing out this generation, and of course, more than 100 benchmarks covering everything from Python performance to HPC. AMD Zen 6 microarchitecture breakdown AMD Zen 6 microarchitecture breakdown (Image credit: AMD) The headline for Zen 6 is a 27% average IPC uplift over Zen 5 in enterprise, cloud, and AI workloads. The debut of this new microarchitecture is focused on the data center, so you shouldn’t take that 27% IPC improvement as broadly applicable to all workloads. Additionally, AMD arrived at that number by comparing fixed-frequency Zen 5 to Zen 6c with 16 cores. As we’ll get into in the next section, a Zen 6c CCD can comfortably fit 16 Zen 6c cores with room to spare, while 16 Zen 5 cores are split across two CCDs. The compute die is built on TSMC’s N2P node, which is an already optimized version of N2 that comes with a 5% performance improvement. Compared to N3E (Zen 5 used N4P), N2P offers an 18% speed improvement at iso-power, or a 36% reduction in power at the same speed. Speed Improvement (v. N3E) Power Improvement (v. N3E) Density (v. articles.title: Reddit Is Turning User Conversations Into AI-Powered Product Reviews
articles.content: Reddit is rolling out an AI-powered shopping feature called "Reddit Reviews" that summarizes user conversations about products and turns them into dedicated reviews. TechCrunch reports: Reddit's announcement points to its rules and its latest measures to combat automated abuse and spam, as well as its practice involving community moderators, as tools it will use to keep the reviews on the site legit. The Reddit Reviews feature itself taps into AI to organize the conversations people are having where they describe their product experiences. These posts will often see users discussing how a product works for them, or why it fails, or what the trade-offs are that someone should consider before buying. The company has been testing the product reviews feature since February, initially with U.S. users in areas like Electronics, Video Games, and Health & Beauty products. In September, Reddit expanded the test to include the Home & Garden and Fashion & Apparel categories as well. Now, the company says Reddit Reviews is rolling out to all U.S. users on iOS, Android, and web, with an initial selection focused on around 10,000 products. Over time, it will roll out to more categories and expand beyond the U.S. To use the feature, Reddit users can search for a product or category in the app's search bar or click on a highlighted product name they see in someone's comment. From there, the user is taken to a screen where important conversations are summarized under a "what people are saying" heading. This will also include a visual breakdown that shows how many of those comments are positive, negative, or mixed, and what sort of things people said they liked or disliked about the item. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review. BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams. Why conventional automation and systems weren’t enough TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow. TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting. To run these agents, TCS chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Three capabilities drove the decision. First, Amazon Bedrock offers a choice of models, so each agent uses the model that fits its task, such as scenario design or code generation, and TCS can adopt newer models as they become available. Second, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scales with demand, so testers across many tenants can run generation and execution sessions at the same time without TCS provisioning or tuning agent servers. Third, the runtime runs each session in its own isolated microVM, which gives TCS session-level separation for its multi-tenant platform without having to build that layer itself. Together, these capabilities let TCS focus its engineering effort on testing logic rather than agent infrastructure, which shortened the time to bring the platform to its BFSI clients. Solution overview The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the platform across five stages, with a per-tenant security layer underneath. Inputs from Jira, business requirement documents (BRDs), and GitLab enter a tenant web application that runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind Amazon CloudFront , with sign-in through Amazon Cognito . TCS uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to host the platform’s specialized agents, built with the Strands Agents SDK . These agents generate the tests, refine them with the tester, and manage their execution. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) runs the generated tests. articles.title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
articles.content: If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call. You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s. We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it. What Amazon Bedrock visibility do you have today? Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging , and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock . It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch . The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you. What is the Amazon Bedrock observability data lake? A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch . Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose , and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization. Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock invocation observability data lake architecture across a central account and linked accounts Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code using two AWS CloudFormation templates, so you can roll it out repeatably across every account in your organization. This can be found in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . What does each Amazon Bedrock invocation log capture? After we run this solution, you will have a combined set of data across the linked account you deploy to so you can query with Athena. What you get per invocation after the logs are flattened into the processed table: The prompt the user or application sent. The model response that came back. Input and output token counts , so you can measure the true weight of each call. The model used, so you can understand utilization of models across teams. The stop reason (for example, max_tokens ), which tells you when a response was cut off. The account and timestamp , so you can attribute and time-slice everything. The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role , so you can see who sent the prompt. After every invocation is captured like this, you go from “We used X tokens on Amazon Bedrock” to “Here is exactly what each model calls contained, and how efficient it was.” That’s the visibility platform and ML teams have been missing. How is the Amazon Bedrock data lake designed? The data lake moves each invocation through five stages, from the moment Amazon Bedrock writes a log to the point you can query it in Athena. 1. articles.title: Alice Huang reportedly instrumental in securing over $7.5 billion of Nvidia AI GPU imports during three-year relationship with Jensen Huang
articles.content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang , who is also suspected of being a spy working for the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). Now, an investigation by The Information has revealed a 'labyrinth' of companies centered around Shanghai Century Litong and connected to Singaporean firm Megaspeed, which has previously been accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. The report claims Alice Huang helped move 240,000 banned chips into the country, mostly H100 and H200 systems, and was instrumental in securing AI GPU imports to the tune of $7.5 billion. Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc) While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push Huawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained Sources in the report link the two companies to Alice Huang via their personal knowledge and corporate registration records, while there have also been reports that some of the Nvidia AI chips Megaspeed bought went to Shanghai Century Litong’s data centers in China. But aside from these corporate ties, there were also numerous reports about Ms. Huang’s personal relationship with the Nvidia chief, and how it gave her the ability to procure chips that were otherwise hard to get elsewhere. Ms. Huang allegedly boasted about her access to the Nvidia CEO publicly. People familiar with her said that she regularly uploaded photos with Jensen to her WeChat account and even shared other images with customers to establish her credibility. She even claimed that Jensen Huang would often celebrate her birthday with dinner and gifts, while an Nvidia China sales employee said that she was a familiar face at the company’s annual event for local Chinese partners. When AI shipments hit delays or faced some trouble, Ms. Huang allegedly would step in to get them moving through the supply chain again. One other person who knows her said that she would often cite her close relationship with Nvidia and its suppliers as the reason why she could always get Nvidia AI chips. It’s estimated that $4.6 billion worth of AI chips have been imported through Megaspeed from 2023 to 2025, with another $2 billion routed through Speedmatrix. It was also reported that Shanghai Century Litong bought GPUs from other sources, with the assistance of Alice Huang if the orders faced an issue, with the total value of the GPUs acquired estimated to be around $7.5 billion. The report claims Ms. Huang helped move some 240,000 banned chips into China. Alice Huang may have appeared in Jensen Huang’s circle much earlier than previously believed. One source told the publication that Kang Wei, Alice Huang’s husband, met Jensen Huang during the 2010s, when Nvidia was primarily a PC gaming GPU manufacturer. According to the report , Kang Wei was a private equity investor focusing on videogame companies back then. In contrast, Ms. Huang reportedly worked for two media companies in China, although some say that there were no records of her doing so. She eventually jumped into banking and finance, working at HSBC and then CITIC Securities, before finally entering the data center industry in 2023 with Megaspeed’s pivot and the founding of Shanghai Century Litong. Shanghai Century Litong is a data center operator founded in June 2023 by a shareholder that was ultimately under the control of Huang Yu, the sister of Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le. The company then provided compute capacity to AI tech giants in China, including Alibaba, Tencent, and other smaller labs. articles.title: Google says Gemini 4 Carbon proved Signal’s encryption in weeks
articles.content: Google released Gemini 4 Carbon to paying developers Tuesday , positioning its newest frontier model above Gemini 4 Argon for complex software engineering, cybersecurity, and scientific reasoning. Argon remains Google’s recommended model for everyday engineering and knowledge work. while Carbon is designed for more demanding tasks, including multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem debugging, and long-horizon agentic workflows. Koray Kavukcuoglu , SVP of Google DeepMind and Google’s chief AI architect, described Carbon in the launch announcement as the company’s strongest model for complex, multi-step work. The release also introduces /swarm , a preview feature in Google Antigravity that coordinates multiple coding agents from a single prompt. Multi-agent coding arrives Carbon can build, test, and debug full-stack applications, checking both the code and rendered UI. Google says it performs particularly well on multi-package migrations and debugging across subsystems. What Google hasn’t explained is how /swarm shares context between agents, handles conflicting changes, or decides which tasks need Carbon instead of a lighter model. Google claims Carbon ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR and Zapier’s AutomationBench, completing tasks at less than half the cost of the next-best model. What Google hasn’t explained is how /swarm shares context between agents, handles conflicting changes, or decides which tasks need Carbon instead of a lighter model. Pricing doubles November 30 The company hasn’t provided enough detail to independently verify those cost comparisons. Carbon launches at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, matching Argon, before doubling to $4 and $20 after November 30. Whether Carbon’s performance offsets those higher costs, including the overhead of multi-agent orchestration and verification, remains to be seen in production. Proving Signal’s code One of the more technically ambitious examples in Google’s announcement involves AlphaProof Code, a new agentic framework for formal verification. Google researchers used Carbon alongside other models to mathematically prove key security properties of the code underlying Signal’s cryptographic protocol. The researchers translated security requirements into mathematical theorems and used AlphaProof Code agents to generate millions of lines of Lean , a language used to express and check mathematical proofs. Google says the work took weeks, compared with the years that similar verification efforts have historically required from expert teams. The announcement doesn’t specify the full scope of the verified properties, how much human intervention it required, or whether Google will make the proof artifacts publicly available. Google says the work took weeks, compared with the years that similar verification efforts have historically required from expert teams. Security that cuts both ways Google initially made Carbon’s cybersecurity capabilities available to selected defenders through its Fairwind Program in late October. The company says Carbon leads on SEC-bench Pro, ExploitGym and CWE-bench v1, benchmarks covering vulnerability discovery, exploitation and patching. In Project Fortify, Google’s autonomous scanning, triage and remediation system, Carbon achieved 100% scanning recall and 95% triage precision on an internal benchmark. Google also reports a relative improvement of more than 25% over Argon’s recall rate when testing open-source repositories. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research team used Carbon to confirm that two bugs in a popular open-source project could be exploited, prompting maintainers to classify them as critical and release patches. articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Open Source Commitment With OpenShell Donation and New AI Infrastructure
articles.content: Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing. To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon , the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities. NVIDIA is contributing NVIDIA OpenShell , an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide. NVIDIA is also contributing to Agent Substrate , an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox. Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform : NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine , NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and NVIDIA Snapshot . These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories. Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future. Securing AI Agents in the Open NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF puts security infrastructure for autonomous agents in the community’s hands to build, inspect and improve — accelerating development and hardening its safeguards. “The cloud-native community has a new infrastructure challenge: giving agents secure environments in which to operate,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. “NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF gives developers a shared foundation to build on and an opportunity to shape how agent security evolves. Bringing this work into the community enables broader collaboration on infrastructure that will be critical to the next generation of cloud-native applications.” OpenShell gives organizations control over what AI agents can do. It applies deterministic controls to agent activity, so teams can enforce policies as agents use tools, access inference services and execute workloads. Its extensible architecture lets teams connect their own compute, inference providers, credential storage and monitoring tools. This allows organizations to apply governance across different deployment environments while integrating OpenShell with their existing enterprise systems. Hundreds of organizations have put OpenShell to use, and the project has received tens of thousands of contributions in less than a year since launch. Scaling Agent Execution on Kubernetes Governing agents is only part of the challenge. Organizations also need to deploy them at scale. NVIDIA is contributing to Agent Substrate, a Google -originated project in the CNCF Sandbox, and ensuring it works with NVIDIA Dynamo for model inference and KAI Scheduler for shared cluster resource allocation. This effort brings together agent execution, inference serving and resource scheduling on Kubernetes. Agent Substrate preserves agent environments between tasks while releasing compute when agents are idle. By suspending and resuming those environments across a shared pool of agents, it lets teams scale agent workloads without keeping dedicated compute running for every session. NVIDIA and Google are also collaborating on an integration of OpenShell and Agent Substrate, so enterprises can secure and govern agents across clouds and on-premises systems. Building an Open Foundation for AI Factories AI factories need to offer customers managed Kubernetes services while retaining control of their infrastructure, software and customer experience. articles.title: The best strategy to protect against getting hacked is surprisingly old-school
articles.content: The recent reports of artificial intelligence agents gone rogue —hacking into corporate systems without being told to by the humans who manage them—are enough to make any systems administrator’s hair stand on end. The increasingly powerful abilities of frontier and other advanced AI models, combined with the apparent inabilities of their creators to keep them caged, have only added to the worries of companies already wrestling with how to protect themselves against AI -armed attackers. Cybercriminals of all kinds are using AI tools in much the same way legitimate organizations do, boosting their productivity and moving their operations from human to machine speed. Meanwhile, businesses have understandably embraced AI themselves. But every new AI tool or application a company chooses to roll out comes with its own security risks. When it comes to AI, many companies feel like they have to take an “adopt or die” business perspective, says Leslie Nielsen , executive vice president and chief information security officer at Mimecast. “They think everybody’s going to pass them by,” Nielsen says. “But then the other side is, if you adopt too fast, it’s adopt and die, right?” While AI threats may be rapidly advancing , so are AI-powered defenses. And experts say following old-school best practices can go a long way toward protecting against even the most advanced attackers. Make sure you’ve got the basics covered The tactics used by AI attackers aren’t a whole lot different from those of human-powered adversaries, they’re just faster and more efficient, Nielsen says. As a result, the fundamentals of defense don’t need to be much different either. “It’s all the basic stuff you should be doing anyway,” he says. “It just becomes more important because the attacks are faster and the attacks are cleaner and more successful sometimes.” That means making sure that access to sensitive data is limited to those who actually need it; immediately patching security vulnerabilities when they become known; and making sure that all critical data is backed up and accessible if needed. And of course, follow the absolute basics, like making sure your cybersecurity defenses require strong passwords and multifactor authentication, and that you’re screening for phishing emails. Just like the attackers, defenders need to bolster themselves with AI tools to speed up their responses, Nielsen says. He added that this is especially true for small- and medium-size businesses that are probably working with smaller security teams. Complicating this already hefty task is the ability of advanced AI models to chain together low-level vulnerabilities into previously undiscovered exploits that could be used to breach a system, says Simon Jelley , vice president of product management at Dell Technologies. “But those risks have always been there,” Jelley says. “It’s just accelerating those exposures and also making AI ultimately smarter.” Lock down your own AI The AI tools used by companies can end up being the insider threats that no one thinks about, experts say. In the case of the AI models gone rogue, it appears they weren’t trying to do anything malicious, just accomplish the objectives set out by their human creators at all costs. “The difference between AI and a person is AI is the eager intern that’s going to do what you ask, but it’s going to keep working 24-seven to get it done, and it’s going to do everything it needs to do,” Nielsen says. That could include doing things like digging up login credentials and accessing data it shouldn’t, potentially putting that data at risk of exposure. That’s why it’s important that there are guardrails in place to keep AI agents on task and to limit their access to sensitive data. articles.title: SpaceXSI quietly flips Grok API text watermarking to off by default
articles.content: The thorny issue of watermarking AI-generated text took an interesting turn this past week, with SpaceXSI seemingly U-turning on plans to automatically watermark text generated by its Grok AI models . As per its updated output watermarking documentation , Elon Musk’s AI company — which recently rebranded from SpaceXAI — says the feature is now off by default, with developers able to enable it for individual models through their team’s administration settings. News of the watermarking feature itself started to emerge in late October, though there was no formal public announcement. The earlier version of the documentation , captured for posterity by the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine on both November 1 and November 6, was quite different to the existing one, noting that watermarking would be on by default starting from November 7. The pending change was spotted by some X users on October 31. SpaceXSI is introducing text watermarking across its Grok API models, starting November 7, 2026 All text outputs from supported Grok models will include a watermark by default Models included: • Grok 4.7 • Grok 4.6 • Grok 4.5 • Grok 4.3 • Grok 4.20 Reasoning • Grok 4.20… pic.twitter.com/wJiuPSEuUH — X Freeze (@XFreeze) October 31, 2026 SpaceXSI has now reversed course, however, making watermarking an opt-in feature for developers using Grok through its API. One online documentation archiving service, Spybara, indicates that the change happened some time between Monday night (November 9) and Tuesday morning (November 10), suggesting that the documentation continued to describe watermarking as enabled by default for nearly three days after its scheduled November 7 rollout. “SpaceXSI has now reversed course, however, making watermarking an opt-in feature for developers using Grok through its API.” The company has given no public explanation for the change, and it’s unclear whether the original default-on policy ever fully came into effect. Meeting the watermarking obligations To rewind just a little, text watermarking is a technique for embedding an invisible, machine-readable signal into AI-generated text. The process subtly influences which words or tokens a model chooses when generating a response, and over a sufficiently long passage of text, those choices create a statistical pattern that can be detected later, helping to establish whether it originated from an AI model. Detection typically requires access to specialised tools, with the major model labs restricting access to their watermark detectors to approved applicants. The technology has become increasingly relevant in Europe, where the EU AI Act introduced transparency obligations for providers of AI systems that generate synthetic content. Under Article 50(2) , providers must ensure that AI-generated text, images, audio and video are marked in a machine-readable format, with the relevant provisions taking effect on August 2, 2026 . A subsequent amendment introduced a limited grace period until December 2 for systems already on the market before August 2, meaning that the clock is ticking for AI companies yet to meet the requirements. It’s worth noting that the various AI companies have taken different approaches to their text watermarking obligations. In August, Anthropic became one of the first major AI labs to announce text watermarking, applying the feature globally across supported Claude models and products, including its API. The decision proved somewhat controversial, particularly among developers concerned about how watermarking might affect generated code , and the fact that Anthropic provided no mechanism for opting out. Meanwhile, OpenAI followed suit in October , introducing its own text watermarking system called textGrain. articles.title: Zyphra Releases ZONOS3-Mini: Open-Source TTS With 100M Active Parameters
articles.content:
Zyphra has released ZONOS3-Mini , an open-source text-to-speech model built for real-time use on local devices. The ZONOS3-Mini text-to-speech model is a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) with 800M total and 100M active parameters. It supports zero-shot voice cloning and word-level delivery control. Weights ship under Apache 2.0. For AI devs, size is the key point. It runs in a browser tab, on a laptop or on a server GPU. TL;DR Size: 800M total parameters, about 100M active per token (64 experts, top-2 routing); 32,768-position context; up to 10 minutes of audio per generation. Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via SGLang-Omni, Apple Silicon via MLX, CPU/CUDA/Metal/Vulkan via ggml, and phones or laptops via WebGPU in the browser. Performance: Ranks first among open models on Zyphra’s ZTTS2-Eval Capability Index (self-reported). Best: 80 ms median time to first audio on one H100 at 8 concurrent requests, and 457 seconds of audio per second peak throughput. Worst: Under 570 ms time to first audio in the browser on a Pixel 9, versus under 150 ms on an M3 MacBook Air. Bottom line: Best: frontier-level open TTS quality at 100M active parameters. Worst: every benchmark is run by Zyphra itself, and reference-clip cloning scores far lower than embedding mode. What is ZONOS3-Mini? ZONOS3-Mini is a compact zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model from Zyphra that runs in real time on-device. Zyphra trained it on 112 NVIDIA H100s in 2.5 days. It follows ZONOS2 , which used 8B parameters and an 86 Hz codec. That size limited where ZONOS2 could be deployed. How does the ZONOS3-Mini architecture work? Zyphra changed 3 layers of the stack : A new codec : Zyphra trained Zyphra Audio Codec 1 (ZAC-1) to replace the Descript Audio Codec. ZAC-1 runs at 15 Hz with 10 codebooks of 4,096 entries: 1 semantic and 9 acoustic. Zyphra reports a 10x word error rate reduction versus a DAC-trained model under similar data constraints. A causal iSTFT head renders each frame to 44.1 kHz audio as soon as it is generated. A hybrid MoE backbone : The model card lists 11 layers with model dimension 1,024. Sequence mixing follows a 3:1 ratio: 9 Gated DeltaNet layers and 2 global attention layers. Zyphra also adds latent MoE, Q balancing and attention residuals. A new speaker encoder : Voice representation moves from the Qwen3-TTS speaker encoder to MECT-B2. The model accepts a raw reference clip of up to 60 seconds, or a single 192-dimensional speaker embedding. Post-training used DPO, then GRPO, to improve robustness. How does word-level voice control work? Identity controls cover age, gender, accent and voice texture through speaker embedding vectors and accent task vectors. Delivery controls cover pace, emotion, projection and liveliness through activation steering. Learned alignment heads let steering apply to specific words during streaming. A separate edit model, based on a VoiceCraft recipe, can modify sentences after generation. Step through
64 experts, top-2 routing. Each token activates 2 experts, so about 100M of the 800M parameters do work per step. That is why the model fits real-time budgets on laptops and phones.
Routing token 1 …
ZONOS2 used 8B parameters on an 86 Hz codec. ZONOS3-Mini cuts both: 800M total, 15 Hz frames.

articles.title: New CNCF report: 75% of cloud-native developers ship code with AI. Jonathan Bryce explains why.
articles.content: Today’s developers are AI-pilled. Cloud native developers even more so. That’s the key takeaway from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s (CNCF) latest report on cloud-native developers , released on Tuesday during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City. The data is clear: As of the third quarter, there were 21.2 million cloud-native developers, or 41% of the total developer population. And while half of non-cloud-native developers use AI to help code, a full three-quarters of their cloud-native peers use AI to ship code today. (Just under two-thirds of all developers using AI to write code use the technology as a central, or core, part of their workflow, according to the dataset.) Why are cloud native developers so comfortable using AI? According to the CNCF ’s executive director Jonathan Bryce , “they’re looking for an edge, they’re looking for an opportunity to work on the latest things and really push the envelope in their career and in their technology use.” Ahead of the report’s release, Bryce sat down with The New Stack to chat all things CNCF and developer trends. And we left the conversation with good news: Alongside a growing developer pool — “more folks are making their way into development roles,” in part-time and full-time fashion, Bryce told TNS — the collection of production-ready tools for the cloud-native developer is rapidly expanding. “More folks are making their way into development roles” Like many open-source software foundations, the CNCF has a tiered approach to adopting, maturing, and releasing new tools. First, there’s the ‘sandbox,’ where projects “develop the kind of rigorous processes that make an open source project trustworthy and predictable and something that you might integrate into a real system,” according to Bryce. Next is the incubation stage, followed by graduation. Of some 250 projects under the CNCF, only a handful reach full graduation. See also: The CNCF is graduating projects faster than ever. AI agents are helping with the due diligence. But their ranks may swell in the coming years. New in the sandbox at CNCF? KubeRay , Agent Substrate , OpenShell , OpenRL , and others. New to incubation? Meshery , K8GB , and others. And KubeVirt , Karmada , and KubeFlow are graduating. Lost amidst the sea of project names? Better do your research. “[W]herever you are in the industry, whatever type of organization you are right now, you need to understand open source technologies because that’s going to give your company leverage options,” Bryce argues. And as we saw from the data we started today with, the number of developers hungry to put the new to work is only getting larger. Our chat covers the Q3 2026 State of Cloud Native Development report, new and graduating projects, the Kubernetes AI Conformance program, and more. Sit back, hit play, and let’s have some fun! articles.title: Secretlab debuts monitor light bar add-on to reduce glare and eye strain
articles.content: Popular gaming chair and gaming desk manufacturer Secretlab has today unveiled its new ErgoArch monitor lightbar , a new lightbar attachment for owners of its Secretlab monitor arm and a complement to its desk ecosystem. Available now, the new lightbar costs $179. Secretlab ErgoArch Monitor Light Bar Add-On For owners or prospective buyers of the Secretlab Magnus Monitor Arm (the light bar is an attachment to this accessory), the ErgoArch provides overhead lighting for your desk and monitor, reducing reflections and glare, and smoothing out brightness contrast between your display and workspace. Monitor light bars are generally designed to reduce eye strain while you're working or gaming, while also providing some snazzy ambient lighting; the ErgoArch is no different. Secretlab says the ErgoArch provides both ultrawide illumination and focused task lighting depending on how you set it up. The lighting itself is smart and can be powered by Nanoleaf, giving you access via your smart home app to 16.8 million colors. There's also a dedicated wireless control puck, and the lighting temperature ranges from 2700K to 6500K. The light itself is mounted to the monitor arm via a three-point adjustment arm and is compatible with any VESA-mounted monitor, including curved displays. There's also a magnetic webcam mount attachment. Power is provided by USB-C, so you don't need a wall outlet or extension socket to switch it on. Available globally, the ErgoArch is available to buy from Secretlab now for $179 .
